notes_list.title: Acidity of Organic Compounds
notes_list.basic_overview: Organic acidity is governed by stability of the conjugate base. Inductive withdrawal, resonance delocalization, electronegativity, hybridization, solvation and aromaticity can all contribute.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For a fixed solvent and comparable structures, rank acids by conjugate-base stability. Electron-withdrawing groups near the acidic center usually increase acidity; resonance-stabilized anions are especially important.
notes_list.examples: Carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols; phenol is more acidic than a typical aliphatic alcohol; terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkenes because the conjugate carbanion is sp-hybridized.
notes_list.conditions_and_medium: Solvent can strongly affect measured acidity because ions are differently solvated. Gas-phase and solution-phase acidity rankings can differ.
notes_list.mechanism_steps: 1. Remove H+. 2. Draw conjugate base. 3. Check resonance. 4. Check inductive effects. 5. Check atom/hybridization/solvation. 6. Rank stabilization.
notes_list.kinetics_and_energy: Acid strength relates to equilibrium ΔG°; pKa is a thermodynamic quantity, not simply a measure of reaction speed.
notes_list.selectivity_and_stereochemistry: High-frequency JAM question type: compare substituted phenols, carboxylic acids, alcohols and hydrocarbons.
notes_list.common_traps: Do not rank acidity only by electronegativity; conjugate-base resonance and solvation can dominate.

exam_focus.level: IIT-JAM / MSc entrance / GATE concept depth
must_revise: lower pKa = stronger acid in same solvent
